utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic, before I give you an opportunity to continue your cross-examination, there's one relatively urgent procedural matter I would like to raise briefly. An application has been made for safe conduct for a future witness. The Chamber would like to know, because this witness is scheduled already on relatively short notice, whether any response will be filed and when it is intended to file such a response, and the Chamber will consider, of course, whether it leave sufficient time to issue the safe conduct, if we decide to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think there's extra microphones on. I can tell you that our position right now is that we will formally file no later than Monday. Our position is that we very much would like to see that witness in the courtroom, and, therefore, we also encourage the Trial Chamber to issue a safe conduct order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On behalf of General Cermak, we have no objection to the application for safe conduct. May this response serve as our filing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the same here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same. So, therefore, the Chamber staff can start drafting. Having dealt with it, Ms. Botteri, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Misetic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me start by going back to this issue about the commission that you were questioned about extensively by the Prosecutor. The commission also had, as its members, members of the military police, and my question to you is: You are aware, are you not, that that component of the commission, meaning the military police, in fact, did have powers to investigate unknown perpetrators. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've talked yesterday a little bit about this order that General Gotovina wrote pursuant to the order from General Cervenko; and in your statement to the Defence, we also talked about this a little bit, you had said that an order from General Gotovina to the military police would not be relevant, and you were asked some questions about that yesterday. Let me show you first Exhibit P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, as can you see on the screen, Ms. Botteri, are the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could, Mr. Registrar, turn to Article 66 of this. It's pages 27 to 28 of the English translation excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this -- these are the rules that govern the work of the military police; and in Article 66, it says: "On the basis of the information gathered, when there are grounds for suspicion that a crime was committed, an authorised official of the military police shall draft a criminal report providing a description of the crime and listing the evidence obtained during the process of information-gathering."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to Article 69, which is the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Article 69 says: "When a report is submitted to an authorised official of the military police by military personnel or someone else, he ... is required to accept the report and forward it without delay to the State Prosecutor in charge, as well as gather the necessary information and take other measures relating to the reported crime and the perpetrator." Now, you said in your Defence statement that an order from General Gotovina would be -- would not be relevant. Is the reason for that, Ms. Botteri, because the military police was already under a legal obligation once it received information to file criminal reports? In other words, they didn't need an additional order from anyone to file a criminal report once they received information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's their obligation arising from the very rules governing the work of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when your commission completed its work and identified members of the 4th Guards Brigade who had illegally entered some apartments in Split, once that information had been obtained, the obligation of the military police to file criminal reports was automatic by virtue of their obligations under the rules. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And any order from General Gotovina or anyone else was superfluous, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to speak closer or into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have a P1007, please, and if we could go to Article 31, please, which is -- it's page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, we talked -- you talked a little bit with the Prosecutor about various articles of the Code of Military Discipline. We didn't talk about Article 31. Article 31 states, as follows: "In situations where the authorised officer finds that the offence against military discipline is also a criminal offence, that [sic] case shall be sent via regular channels to the authorised Prosecutor; if he thinks that it is in the interest of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary proceedings [sic]." Now, in practice, Ms. Botteri, what this meant was that an act which had the elements of a crime was something that should -- would first be referred to the military prosecutor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, as I read this provision, the intent is that, generally, military commanders are not to undertake disciplinary proceedings for acts that are -- have elements of criminality, but are to refer it to the prosecutor; however, there is an exception, which is if the authorised officer makes the subjective determination that it is in the interests of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary proceedings. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you were aware that you included some four or five rather complex legal issues, and a simple "yes" by the witness, of course, must be of comfort to you, but is, of course, not really --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm getting into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, let's break this down. Would you agree with me, based on your experience working in the Split Military District, that one of the policy issues underlying this provision was that you did not want commanders to be opening up their own investigations and, thus, potentially disrupting a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what might happen if a criminal investigation was under way and a commander whose subordinates may be involved in a criminal act then was authorised to start conducting his own investigations? What was the danger there that could occur, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you know, what -- what potentially could happen if a military commander, generally speaking, was able to start launching parallel investigations concerning discipline while a criminal investigation was under way by the military police? Let me put it more directly. Was there a potential that by launching a parallel investigation you could disrupt evidence in the criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this provision in Article 31 that says: "If he thinks that it is in the interest of the service, he shall also initiate disciplinary procedures." You were the person in charge with interpreting the Code for General Gotovina. Correct? You were his legal advisor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How do you interpret that provision? Does that provision obligate a commander to undertake disciplinary proceedings, or does that provision allow him to subjectively to determine whether disciplinary proceedings are needed?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provision does not obligate a commander but, rather, empowers him to assess for himself whether it would be in the interests of the service to initiate a disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to the commission, General Cervenko, in his initial order, says he wants, in addition to the criminal reports being filed, he wants disciplinary measures to be taken. Is that something that, under Article 31, General Cervenko was authorised to do in his subjective determination?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He would be authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Article 31 in practice and about forming commissions generally. If, under Article 31, the commander as a general rule is not supposed to interfere in a criminal investigation by launching a disciplinary investigation, obviously concerning acts that also have elements of criminality, then if a commander were to launch an inquiry concerning a disciplinary violation that was also a crime, at the end of that inquiry, as a general rule, he would, nevertheless, have to then abstain and refer the matter to the military prosecutor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me show -- I'm going to show you, Ms. Botteri -- it's in English, so I will read some portions of it. This is from an expert report by an expert the Prosecution is using, named Reynaud Theunens. I am going to show you what Mr. Theunens said about the military police, what role it had. This is page 89 of the Theunens report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'll not be tendering this into evidence; I'm just using it for demonstrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens in describing the authority of the military police says, and you can read the yellow highlighting: "The members of the military police can apply the following measures while performing their tasks: Warning, identification, report, bringing in," and then it goes on. Then when you go to subpart 2, below, in defining what "report" means, Mr. Theunens says: "Reporting concerns the submission by the members of the military police of disciplinary reports against military personnel who have violated military discipline and of a criminal report against persons who have committed a crime that falls within the jurisdiction of a military court." Now, Ms. Botteri, what this means is that it was the military police, in conducting a criminal investigation, when they arrived at a perpetrator and identified him, not only did the military police file a criminal report but it was the military police who would then file a report with the authorised body, whether it be the commander or the military disciplinary court, so that disciplinary proceedings could also be taken, if necessary. Correct? Let me shorten the question. The military police conducts criminal investigations. At the end of that criminal investigation, the military police was to not only file a criminal report but also had an obligation to file a disciplinary report with the appropriate body so that disciplinary measures could also be taken. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if a commander believes that the military police is investigating an act which can be or is classified as s crime, it was understood, was it not, that the military police would also ensure that disciplinary measures would be -- a disciplinary report would also be filed after that investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In other words, there should have been no need to open up separate investigations for disciplinary violations that also have elements of criminality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. In none of the cases was this -- has this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me make sure we're -- we're talking about the same thing. My point, Ms. Botteri, is that if the military police was conducting a criminal investigation, the disciplinary investigation was subsumed within that investigation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, as a general rule, there was no need for commanders to open up their own investigations concerning acts that were also subject to criminal investigation by the MPs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not necessary at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I noted the difference in phrasing of your previous question, that earlier you asked whether there should have about no need; whereas, now you're asking there was no need, which, of course is not the same. I just want you to be aware that I noticed this difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can ask it either way judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There should have been no need to conduct a separate investigation for matters that were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue being that what should be and what was is not the same, depending on factual circumstances. There should be no need to create food aid programmes if every state would take its responsibility to feed its own population, which does not mean that there is no need to create such programmes, depending on what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm emphasizing this because, as you may have noticed also in the earlier stages of the examination of this witness, I very much insisted on making it a clear distinction what should be there or what was the system and what happened. I emphasise this, that the Chamber is not only interested in knowing whether there should be no need but whether there was no need. You see the point, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do, but let me see if I can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just leave it to you. Of course, I could remain silent and say nothing about it, but I think sometimes it is good if counsel is aware of what comes to the mind of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, you've heard the comments of the Presiding Judge, so let me ask you this question. The commission was formed concerning the apartments because somebody came to General Gotovina, specifically General Cervenko, to say that the usual procedure - in other words, what should happen - isn't going to happen here, for whatever reasons that General Cervenko determined, so you need to do the following. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that if some sector of the Croatian system was unable to do what it should be doing, and they needed General Gotovina's intervention, that what would happen is somebody would bring it to General Gotovina's attention, correct, just as happened with General Cervenko. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Unless somebody brought it to General Gotovina's attention that the different sectors of the Croatian system were not going to be doing the tasks which they typically are supposed to be doing, General Gotovina and you, in his command, would assume that the system is functioning as it should. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into one microphone or the other but not both. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see how attractive it to be heard twice, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm either not heard in one or too heard in two so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll overcome this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll cut his one in half, maybe that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, let me show you a different passage from Mr. Theunens' report, and this is page 160 and we will also show it via sanction concerning what military discipline refers to. This is again page 160, where Mr. Theunens writes: "Military discipline refers to the exact, full, and timely conduct of military service." Now, you were the person in charge or in the legal department of the Split Military District. Military discipline is primarily concerned with ensuring exactly what Mr. Theunens says here: "The exact, full, and timely conduct of military service." Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is not primarily concerned with ensuring that every perpetrator of a crime meets justice. Correct? It is intended to protect the army not to necessarily punish the individual. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the criminal justice system that is intended to mete out punishment to the individual primarily. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll be getting back to that in a few minutes, but let me also turn your attention to Article 26 -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, let me call up 65 ter 929, Mr. Registrar. Actually -- all right. That's fine. While I was there, I was going use it, but that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, you were asked some questions about subordination as well. I just want to show you the order by the then-chief of the Main Staff of the 3rd of July 1995, General Bobetko, in which the 7th Guards Brigade was, and I quote: "Operatively resubordinated to the ZP Split."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, and if we can go to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And they create -- it says: "I make the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade and the commander of the Split Military District personally responsible for the implementation of this order, and they shall report to me following implementation of the order through the chain of command." Do you have any -- are you familiar with the fact that operatively the 7th Guards Brigade was resubordinated to the Split Military District in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may have I this exhibit marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D880 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your Defence statement, you talked about how -- you said at paragraph 14: "The Split Military District could not have conducted disciplinary proceedings against members of the attached subordinated units; that is, it could have conducted them in extraordinary cases, but the system was not set up to suit such cases." I would like to talk to you for a few minutes about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go back to P1007, please, at Article 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, I'm going to advise the Chamber that this is an translation issue in Article 26. There are words missing in the English translation that are in the Croatian original. So if I could ask Ms. Botteri to just -- or I will read out the relevant passage that's missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ask her to read slowly, and you know that it's not the task of our interpreters to correct translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, to close our eyes for that is also a bit stupid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if you would please read the relevant short passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will start just the -- the clause that talks about -- it begins in the English, "If such measures are," which is the third line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "If they are required and necessary for maintaining order and discipline."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the translation by our interpreters, could you please have the translation verified on this issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, the word was translated as "necessary" and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know what the system is. It can be read again, a translation issued, but we are not whispering in the ears of our interpreters what the correct interpretation should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not what I'm saying. In order for me to proceed with the examination, there's an element of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you use the original text --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then put questions in relation to the original text, then I take it the right answer will emerge, if that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In Croatian, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you are seeking interpretation of this legal provision, then I think there's nothing wrong in quoting the original, and then we'll hear and you will hear what the translation is. And if there's any issue as usual, we do not have a debate on translation, but then, of course, during the break if is not resolved in such a way that we can deal with it, then during the break there will certainly be a possibility to resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me also for the record say that the interpretation is not incorrect. It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you know better --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I have to clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, the phrase in Article 26, "potrebiti u nuzni," now can you explain to us what you understand by the word "nuzni." What does that mean in this context? If could you help us out, because it is not in the English translation on our screen.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where such conduct is involved that necessarily calls for intervention in order to prevent any such conduct that would -- or, rather, to prevent continued unlawful conduct on the part of the perpetrator as an emergency measure or an urgent measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's exactly what I wanted to develop with you. It is -- the word there means it is in an emergency situation or in an urgent situation that requires immediate intervention. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emergency intervention or urgent intervention, but we're discussing only disciplinary measures here, not disciplinary sentences. Once again, this goes to show that only more lenient disciplinary measures were applied as emergency interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to exhibits P -- the first exhibit is P1014, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, there has been a question on my mind for quite a while. I'll phrase the question and then if you will deal with it anyhow, then I'm not asking for an answer at this moment; however, if not, I would like to invite the witness to answer that question. Ms. Botteri, Article 26 deals with measures to be taken to offenders who are not members of their organic unit. Now, just for my understanding, I can imagine two situations. The one is that a commander happens to see a soldier committing a disciplinary offence, a soldier with whom he who is got nothing to do, apart from the fact that he sees it happening. You're going deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That first part, yes. I don't know what your second part is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second, of course, is that even on a temporary basis, there has been created a command relationship, an operational command relationship. If that is it a matter that will you deal with, then I'll not ask the witness at this moment to answer this question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, we're about to go into now answering Judge Orie's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we could go to P1014, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is what you were shown on direct examination. It concerns the disciplinary measure issued directly by General Gotovina to members of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade which was not organically part of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn the page, please, and again if we could go -- sorry. If we could go back to the first page, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: While we are there at that first page, I wanted to follow-up with you on something that you explained yesterday. This is the Split Military District, sending to the chief of the Main Staff, General Gotovina's personal disciplinary measure. Is that because of the principle that we established yesterday? In other words, the next highest ranking commander above General Gotovina would have been the chief of the Main Staff; and, therefore, it was up to the chief of the Main Staff to evaluate the disciplinary measure issued by General Gotovina. Is that correct? Did you understand my question, Ms. Botteri?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand your question and my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this describes what happened. And if we go to paragraph 3, it says that: "He admitted to having entered the area of disengagement on 17 May 1995, and that he is aware of the fact that, by doing so, he might have jeopardized himself and others." Then it goes on explaining the rational for issuing the disciplinary measure. Now, the fact that General Gotovina is the -- well, first, let me take a step back. This situation, if you can determine from the text, involved a situation where these members of an attached subordinated unit entered, in violation of orders, entered the zone of separation between the warring sides. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And by doing that, they, through their conduct, could have caused hostilities to begin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And by virtue of that, they could have cost the lives of soldiers as well as civilians who would have been subjected to a conflict that would break out as a result of their entering the zone of separation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, first, is that the type of situation under Article 26 that is the emergency urgent measure that needs to be taken on the spot?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a typical example of an urgent intervention and an emergency application of this Article 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Gotovina, by virtue of the fact that he is the commander issuing the discipline as a matter of first instance, does that suggest to you that it was General Gotovina who personally observed this disciplinary infraction?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, now, to get to the Presiding Judge's question, this is one of those exceptions to the rule that you yourself described in your statement. You said, in extraordinary circumstances, it could happen that a commander would issue a disciplinary measure against a subordinated -- an attached subordinated unit. Is this one of those extraordinary measures that were called for under Article 26 of the Code of Military Discipline?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This was -- this measure was not undertaken simply because the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade was now a subordinated part of the Split Military District and, therefore, was generally subject to disciplinary measures issued by the Split Military District Command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, have you dealt with the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because I would have some questions. Ms. Botteri, a few questions in relation to this. First of all, could you tell us under what circumstances it was established that this guard member committed this mistake? When was it established; when it happened or afterwards, or what were the circumstances? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is not clear to me, under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I mean is, was he caught in the act being seen by his colleagues or was it reported three days after the event had happened? That's what I mean by the circumstances, and how was it established, what way was it established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now another thing that we see is that in this order, no reference is made to Article 26; whereas, I understand from your answer that Article 26 of the rule book seems to be the basis for the competence to issue this order. Do you have any explanation of not mentioning apparently a vital element --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your question, but I would have to look at Articles 27 and 33, the ones that are referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we discussed earlier that you called this a typical example of the exercise of authority or competence under Article 26; nevertheless, it's not mentioned here as the basis for this decision. Have you any explanation for the absence of any reference to Article 26?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be an error, but also I'm unable to reply to the question with precision because I don't know what Articles 22 and 33 of the rule book say, or Article 4 of the addition to the rule book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my last question in relation to this document is the following: The offence is described, the seriousness of it is described, it is described that this should not remain without consequences. The emergency to issue this disciplinary measure, I do not read it, but do I miss anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that you've missed anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify some more of that, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D58-0052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Ms. Botteri, this is a letter that you wrote to your superiors in the legal affairs administration in Zagreb in the Ministry of Defence on the 14th of August, 1995, so ten days after Operation Storm began. It is, on its face, a response apparently to a request from the legal affairs administration that you submit proposed changes to the Code of Military Discipline. And while we're on the first page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Ms. Botteri, this is the fifth paragraph in the Croatian version. First, if you could explain to us why one of your proposed changes was that: "The text of the Code needs to be corrected in a manner to exclude the use of terms such as a disciplinary offence and mistake, but use only one single term, and along with specific definitions of a disciplinary offence and a disciplinary violation to establish at least the basic criteria for the differentiation of one breach from the other, in order to unify the practice of the HV units." Can you explain what motivated to you write that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat this, although I've stated it more than once, breaches of discipline were divided into minor offences and major offences. Any commander, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Military Discipline, starting from the position of platoon commander upwards, could establish by himself the criteria used to determine what was a minor and what was a major offence. In other words, the Code of Military Discipline did not establish any criteria that a commander could use to determine in a uniform manner what sort of unlawful behaviour was in question. And working on this in practice, I felt that, for the same criteria to be applied everywhere and for the proper implementation of the Code of Military Discipline, with a view to upgrading discipline, the Code itself should establish the criteria, so that the practice, the implementation would be uniform throughout the chain of command in the entire Military District. This is what propertied me to ask for amendments to the Code of Military Discipline, to this effect. I did this so that at the level of the command of the Military District, there could be more control and better supervision of the implementation of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in this document, please, and this is now -- it's the first paragraph in the page in Croatian, and it is the, I believe, third paragraph in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you also recommended and state: "We think that the simplest way to deal with disciplinary violations is to implement the principle of territoriality in the manner that all persons serving in the armed forces are subject to disciplinary responsibility to the Military District Commander, i.e., the military disciplinary court pertaining to the Military District." Now, can you explain to the Court what you were trying to convey there by suggesting a change that would adopt the principle of territoriality?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we wanted to achieve was the following: The added tasks that were not in the organic composition - we've often discussed this in the course of my testimony - should also be within the competence of the commander of the Split Military District, as regards military discipline. So all the attached units would be under his command as regards military discipline. That was our proposal for the very reason that, in practice, we noticed deficiencies in this respect. The application of the Code of Military Discipline in the way that it established the competences and jurisdiction of the commander of the Military District made it difficult or even prevented the establishment of total discipline in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of deficiencies you noticed, specific examples of what the deficiencies were? Let me ask a more specific question, Ms. Botteri. We've talked about there principle of the next highest commander reviews a disciplinary measure undertaken by his immediate subordinate. In the concrete case, if the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade, General Ivan Korade, disciplined a member of the 7th Guards Brigade during or after Operation Storm, who was the next commander, the immediate to General Korade, who would review that measure to make sure it was a properly issued disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the commander of the Military District that the 7th Guards Brigade belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that it never happened that a disciplinary measure issued by the 7th Guards Brigade or any other attached unit to the Split Military District had the disciplinary measures of the commander of that attached unit sent to General Gotovina for review?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that one of the deficiencies in the system that you were trying to correct but suggesting the adoption of the principle of territoriality?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It follows from the text. The text itself is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Finally, on this document, Ms. Botteri, is it safe to say by virtue on the fact that on the 14th of August, 1995, by suggesting that the principle of territoriality should be adopted, is it safe to say that it was your understanding as the legal officer in the command that the Split Military District did not have disciplinary authority over attached units? That's the first part of my question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're quite correct. You're completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The second part of my question is: But the Split Military District Command, on the 14th August, was seeking that authority over attached units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D881.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D881 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, again, while we're on this topic, Ms. Botteri, you were shown the statistics from the third quarter of the Split Military District concerning disciplinary measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that is P1017, Mr. Registrar, and if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is the report that you sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, and if we can go to page 4 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: By the way, to follow-up on my last series of questions, Ms. Botteri, did you ever get the authority to have territorial jurisdiction over attached subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our proposals were not adopted by the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I ask one or two additional questions in relation to this. Why did you want to change to another system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Observing the problems that came up in practice. I was a person who, if there was a single incident in practice, would always consider the best way of solving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were the problems in practice? I mean, if in the old system, to say so, or the existing system, everything went well, what were the problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember individual instances, but questions arose coming from subordinate commanders in their daily work and activities. Because these attached units were on our territory, they had questions for me, asking me how to solve this problem, and that's how I assessed the situation and evaluated that the problem could be solved by the application of military discipline, according to the territorial principle. I have to add that, apart from these written traces, we had consultations, workshops; and, as regards what I said about establishing criteria that would lead to uniform practice, when deciding what was a minor and what was a major offence, at each such consultation I requested these changes to be me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be a different subject, the clarification of offences. You said you got questions. Now, I'm just trying to imagine we have a non-organic but temporarily operational part of the Split Military District. Now, if someone commits a disciplinary offence, the commander would take the measures and those measures would be reviewed, either for their regularity or through an appeal by his commander, perhaps outside the Split Military District. What's wrong with that? I mean, what was wrong in the old system? What were these questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Questions had to do with the jurisdiction over troops who were present in the territory of the Split Military District. The system was organised in such a way that whatever instruments were prescribed by the Code of Military Discipline could not be imposed against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the system was not functioning. Is that how I have to under it? Was it just impractical and was it cumbersome to send matters for review to someone who was at totally different place; or was the system not proper functioning, which means that either the issuance of disciplinary measures or regularity reviews of such measures did not take place in accordance with the rules? What was the problem, non-functioning or practical problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree with your statement that the system did not function at all; rather, there were difficulties in practice, especially so when one had attached units to his own troops in an area. The system was well-equipped to function only where no attached units were present as an added asset in a given territory. Generally speaking, the system was functional; however, every system can be improved and perfected. And in our view, the system would have been perfected had the principle of territorial jurisdiction been introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, let's look at what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll to the left, please -- actually, I don't know if it is cut off in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe the same page is on the next page without the margin cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please. Thank you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we see the military police -- or the post codes for the various units; and, yesterday, you told us that given the passage of time you don't recall the various codes. But let me ask you, as a general matter, none of these units are the attached units resubordinated to the Split Military District. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So you, when you would send these reports, had no statistical information whatsoever as to what disciplinary measures were being taken by units that were operationally subordinated to the Split Military District. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Those -- based on your answer to one of my previous questions, those units, when they would send their statistics, they wouldn't send them to you in the Split Military District. They would send their statistics back to their home, so to speak, military districts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when we talk about what types of problems did the non-territoriality create, would one of the problems be that the Split Military District Command was not entitled to receive information about disciplinary measures being undertaken by units that are operating on its territory?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I said. We were unable to control, supervise, or evaluate the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked some questions concerning the military commencing proceedings before the military disciplinary court. You were asked questions about who was the lowest level commander in the Split Military District who could issue a decision to commence those proceedings, and the answer was the Split Military District commander. My question to you, however, is: How did a matter of -- how did a case come to the attention of the military district commander for his review as to whether it should be referred to the military disciplinary court? What was the process by which the commander of the military district is seized of such a case?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer was that the military district commander passed a decision to bring charges against an individual before the military disciplinary court. I wanted to describe the procedure preceding that particular stage; however, I was only asked to give a straightforward answer to the question put to me and which was taken out of the context of the Code of Military Discipline. On this particular issue, it is the company commander who would, as far as I remember, under the Code of Discipline, send a report to the battalion commander, who would, in turn, report -- or, rather, conduct an inquiry on that particular issue and report on that to the brigade commander. I wouldn't like to make a mistake, and I'd like to have a look at the Code of Military Discipline. I believe that the brigade commander would then pass a decision to launch an investigation, and only once the entire investigative procedure was completed would the military district commander render a decision to bring charges before the military disciplinary court and send the decision to the military disciplinary prosecutor. I don't have if I was specific enough but that was the procedure in short, as it went from the company commander via the battalion commander, and the brigade commander through to the military district commander, who, ultimately, was only seized of rendering a decision to -- whereby charges were brought before the court. Throughout the chain of command, it was down to each and every one of the commanders to assess if the unlawful conduct involved amounts to a minor or a major explain offence. As I've just said a moment ago, no criteria existed for that. If a procedure was initiated, based on the assessment made by, for instance, a battalion commander to the effect that the conduct involved was a minor disciplinary offence and if that procedure ended at the level of the brigade, even if subsequently the military district commander were to learn about that particular case, since it already been completed by, at that time, in application of the res iudicata principle, or, rather, that double jeopardy was not allowed, the military district commander could not take any further measures. He was powerless in that. As for us, we would only receive statistical data and were not in a position to enforce full control and supervision over military discipline, precisely due to these provisions contained in the Code of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you. You referred to the fact that the matter then, once, after all of those steps, it even got to the military district commander, he would then refer it to the military district prosecutor. The military disciplinary prosecutor, then, made his own evaluation as to whether to proceed with charges before the military disciplinary court. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If he gave it a green light, then he filed the list of charges or an indictment before the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am about to go into a different topic, so I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we better first have a break. As far as timing is concerned, any changes in respect of the assessment of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a change on my part. I have no questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will take at least the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, may I take it that the third session would be enough for you and perhaps for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I may need a little bit time in the third session, but I anticipate finishing in the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, at paragraph 10 of your Defence statement, you talk about the fact that, and I quote: "Problems with reserve soldiers were, in practice, solved by means of individual demobilization. It was my subjective view that the commanders would rather get rid of their problematic reservists by simply substituting them for another soldier in cooperation with the defence office." Then you go on to say: "For many, this presented a graver punishment than the one prescribed by the Code." Now, first, I'd like to turn your attention to Article 11 of the Code of Disciplinary Conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Registrar, that is P1007, please. It would be page 4 in the English, which is where Article 11 begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your direct examination, you were asked about a few of these types of measure, sentences, that should shall be meted out to servicemen found to be responsible for major violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the fifth -- the fifth different type of sentence was termination -- termination of status as active servicemen. Now, I understand that there's a difference between an active servicemen and a reservist, but in terms of the nature of the disciplinary measure taken against a reservist, do you think that demobilization, because of misconduct, is something that is consist with the spirit of Article 11, in terms of what disciplinary sanctions are appropriate in order to ensure discipline in units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph, 10, of your Defence statement, you said: "Demobilization presented a graver punishment than the one prescribed by the code." Then you said: "In other words, by loosing the status of a mobilized person, the person also lost income ensured to them as a member of the HV." Can you explain, particularly in the circumstances of August 1995, what you meant by a mobilized person losing income as a member of the HV and how that impacted those reservists?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the general social welfare circumstances at the time, to demobilize a reservist meant grave consequences for that person, because at that time a when there was widespread unemployment and financial difficulties, that person would be left without the income that his mobilized status in the Croatian army ensured him. That meant drastic -- that was perceived as a drastic punishment for that person far graver than any other sentence that could have been meted out to that person under the Code of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the demobilization process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 2591, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a few documents before I ask you some questions, Ms. Botteri. This is a decision by the minister of defence on the 9th of August. In point 1, as of 9 August, he says: "Start immediately with demobilization of at least 70.000 conscripts in the units, institutions, and commands of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia ... under the command of the Main Staff of the Croatian army." Point 2 is: "The demobilization of conscript, materiel, and technical equipment from the records and installations shall be carried out until 30 August 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- or, Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D882, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D882 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to 1D58-0048, please. This is now General Cervenko's order to the various military districts, dated 14 August 1995. On the basis of the demobilization instruction from the minister of defence, point 1 says: "Military district commanders shall enable the demobilization of all military conscripts with refugee status who wish to be demobilized." Then it describes how demobilization is to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D883 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could now have 1D58-0062, please. And just for the record, Your Honour, there is no date on this document, but I will follow up with the next document which I think will establish the general date of the document, because there is an subordinate who, on the basis of this order, issues a subordinate order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This an order now from the commander of Operative Group West, which I will later demonstrate was issued on or around 19 August 1995, and it says: "Based on an oral order by the Deputy Commander of the Split Military District, staff Brigadier Ademi with the purpose of improving the control and re-enforcing discipline in the Split MD units ..." Point 1is: "All commanders of the units in the zone of responsibility of Operative Group West can according to their own judgement dismiss part of the soldiers from their own units. Principally dismiss individuals or groups who are behaving in a manner that causes disturbance of discipline and order."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D884, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D884 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D58-0050, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now the order passed on by Mr. Fuzel's [phoen] subordinate. It says: "Based on the memo of the commander of Operative Group West..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the class numbers match the order I just tendered into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... notification," it says, "to dismiss -- may dismiss conscripts from the unit to the order; 2, primarily dismiss the individuals in groups who with their behaviour disturb the order and discipline within the unit and, as such, significantly impair the implementation of combat tasks. It is necessary that the commanders of the units, according to their personal assessment, propose to the Manning and staff division the names of conscripts who need to be demobilized."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D885 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 880, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is also the 19th of August, again within Operative Group West. This is now an order in the 142nd Home Guard Regiment, again referring to the order of the commander of the Operative Group West. Once again, it says: "To demobilize, in the first place ..." -- sorry. "In the first, to discharge individuals or groups that breach discipline an order." Now, Ms. Botteri, you said in your statement that it was your subjective view that commanders were demobilizing soldiers because of disciplinary problems; however, were you aware at the time that there, in fact, were orders to use demobilization as a means of preserving discipline in the units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did say that this was my subjective view; however, my area of work was not closely related to mobilization and demobilization, which is why I said that I was aware of that because I had general knowledge the work going on at the headquarters, at the command. I formed my own opinion of it. This, however, does not mean that I was aware of these orders. It is just that they did not fall within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But the -- my next question to you is: If, in fact, the disciplinary measure that was being imposed was demobilization as reflected in these orders, would individual demobilization of problematic soldiers be reflected in any of the statistics you prepared in your reports about the nature of the disciplinary or the number of the disciplinary measures ... [Overlapping speakers] ...taken?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why they wouldn't be in your statistics?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Demobilization was, in fact, a sanction for the perpetrator involved; however, formally and legally speaking, in the context of the implementation of the Code of Military Discipline, it was not a disciplinary sanction. I kept records only those formally imposed disciplinary sanctions as provided for in the Code of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D886, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D886 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have, while we're still on this topic, 1D58-0045, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is it an order from the commander of the 6th Home Guard Brigade, and it says -- it's 16 August 1995: "Due to unbecoming conduct I hereby order, 1, the demobilization, collection of weapons, and removal from the units payroll for the following member of the command centre, Mario Rejanovic, date of demobilization." Then the order is signed by the commander. Is this the type of measure if demobilization that were referring to in your statement about the type of specific measure that would be taken against reserve soldiers.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that it be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D887 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, I'm going to go through four documents quickly here, and then maybe ask you a couple of questions after them, but in terms of what other measures were being taken in addition to this demobilization process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D58-0001, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order for General Gotovina on the 18th of August, an order on taking security measures for units returning from the battlefield. In the preamble, it says that the order is because of an order from the General of the Main Staff -- the chief of the Main Staff, about reports of certain units on the way back from the battlefield opening infantry fire in inhabited settlements and, thus, endangering the lives and the security of the civilian population and causing disturbance of public order and peace and military discipline. Then there is an order, point 1: "Strictly forbid the return of the units from the battlefield to their home garrisons and peacetime locations prior to an organised collection of storage and all infantry armament, ammunition, and mine explosive devices from the military conscripts."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D888 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next document, Mr. Registrar, is 65 ter 2097, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the commander of the 112th Brigade on 20th of August, again concerning breach of order and discipline and because of the international reputation of the Republic of Croatia. It says: "I hereby order," again this is on the basis of an order the operative group commander, "to establish control in all the unit and immediately take measures against setting fire to facilities and killing animals. Disciplinary and criminal measures are to be taken against any irresponsible individuals."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D889 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D652, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again an order being passed by the commander of the 113th, passing along the same orders, as you can see, again on the 20th of August, again calling for disciplinary measures and the institution of criminal proceedings against responsible individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, Mr. Registrar, now to Exhibit D653, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the commander -- the order of the commander of Operative Group West, 20 August 1995, saying that this order is being passed due to the unidentified lack of order and discipline and in view of the international reputation of the Republic of Croatia, and again to establish control in all units, to take measures against the burning of structures and killing of animals, to take disciplinary and criminal publishes against irresponsible individuals. Then this order says: "The commanders of battalions and independent units must pay particular attention to burning and killing of animals with their subordinated commanders down to the command level of squad, because we will find ourselves in a situation where the army will not have anywhere to camp." Now, Ms. Botteri, were you aware at that time that orders were being passed in this period of 18 to 21, 22 August, up and down the chain of command, concerning establishment of discipline within the units? Were you aware of these types of orders?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it was up to then the commanders of the individual subordinated units to undertake the disciplinary measures necessary to establish order and discipline in the units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've established that one of the measures that was taken was the demobilization of these type of problematic soldiers, but let's talk about something that was highlighted in the direct examination by the Prosecution regarding the high number of disciplinary measures taken for soldiers who were absent without leave. Do you recall that discussion while you were being questioned by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to read a portion of some trial testimony and then show you some documents and ask you some questions. But on the 9th of April, 2008, and on the 11th of April, 2008, we -- this Trial Chamber heard testimony from a witness named Edward Flynn, who was a representative of the human rights action teams that were operating in Sector South. He discussed at transcript pages 1.097, and I'll read to you his testimony. He says on questioning by the Prosecution: "Do you note the paragraph which refers to the burning of houses and seeing two soldiers belonging to the 4th Guards Brigade lounging next to the burning houses?" He answered: "Yes. I wrote that, here, the 4th Split Brigade -- yeah, I remember that. I was present. I saw that." "How did you identify the unit the soldiers belonged to? "You know, at that time, I may have become familiar with the different markings of soldiers from different units, but I may also have relied on one of my colleagues to help me with that information." Then, in trial transcript page 1.321 to 1.322, on my questioning, Mr. Flynn testified that he did not see any armoured vehicles in the vicinity of that village, that these soldiers of the 4th Guards Brigade could have been in -- using civilian transportation, and that he did not see sounds of gun-fire or other visible or audible evidence that there was a military operation taking place. Now, before I ask you questions about that incident, let me show you an order by General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D204, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by General Gotovina on the 10th of August, and in it he writes: "Based on the information from the areas liberated by the HV, the analysis thereof, and in order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct, and to save human life, I hereby order ..." Point 1 is: "I prohibit arbitrary movement of the HV members in the liberated areas without the knowledge of their superior commanders."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to D205, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the commander of the 113th Brigade, after having received General Gotovina's order, issuing that order to his subordinates. In it, the first point, again, is: "I forbid movement of members of the 113th HV Infantry Battalion in the liberated areas without knowledge of the superior commander." Now, first of all, on the basis of those two orders and the fact that that is point 1 in both orders, one of the problems regarding soldiers who may be committing crime is that they were absent from their units and the commanders didn't flow where their soldiers were. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to D192, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's notes: The booths are having problems hearing the counsel. If the lectern could be rearranged in such a way so that the microphone is closer to him please, that would be great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe never has this problem, I note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll refrain from any comment on that, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, this is a request sent by Commander Kotlar. You saw that, on 12 August, he issued an explicit order that commanders were to know where their soldiers were. Now there's a long list of soldiers for whom he is seeking the forcible apprehension. At number 29, one of those soldiers was Vladimir Gojanovic. Apparently, Commander Kotlar does not know where some of the soldiers who are mobilized in his unit are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P200, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gojanovic testified before this Trial Chamber, and this is the demobilization order issued by Commander Kotlar concerning Mr. Gojanovic. It says he is to be demobilized on the 7th of September. Now, I have a few questions for you on the basis of all the documents we've looked at now. IN this particular instance, you see that Mr. Gojanovic is absent from his unit, at least according to Mr. Kotlar; yet, Mr. Gojanovic testified that he never received a disciplinary measure and that the only thing that happened to him at the end was that he was demobilized. Is that consistent with you understand of what types of measures were taken against soldiers such as Mr. Gojanovic who apparently were absent from their units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gojanovic, according to theses document, the commander of the 113th did not know where he was, as well as various other individuals, who were mobilized into the 113th, and the measure that appears to have been taken against Mr. Gojanovic, the only measure, is the demobilization order that is now on your screen. My question to you is: Is that demobilization one of the ways that commanders, such as Commander Kotlar, dealt with individuals who failed to stay in their units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now let's go to the next step. I read you the portion about Mr. Flynn seeing two members of the 4th Guards Brigade next to a burning building without any apparent signs of hostilities or a military operation in the area. Now, yesterday, we established that many disciplinary measures were taken for soldiers who were absent without leave. My question to you is: If a commander knows that his soldier is absent from his unit with but cannot prove what that soldier was doing while he was absent from the unit, what is the disciplinary measure that he can take that he knows he can prove, in addition to demobilization?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was a bad question. A commander who only can prove that his soldier was absent from the unit can only undertake the disciplinary measure of punishing the soldier for being absent from his unit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if he suspects or he has a subjective view that soldier may have been stealing from homes while he was absent from the unit, may have set fire to a house while he was absent from the unit, he can't take a disciplinary measure for those infractions, unless he has evidence that can prove that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A disciplinary measure can refer only to his absence from the unit. By no means you can have disciplinary procedures undertaken for anything the soldier might have done during his absence because there's no proof. It's impossible to conduct the proceedings in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, also, going back to how we started this morning, if, in fact, the suspicion was that what he was doing while he was away from the unit was criminal in nature, that was a matter to be dealt with by the crime police or the military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
