utterances.text: Now, let's talk about how this demobilization -- some of the problems with the demobilization.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So if we could first, Mr. Registrar, go to 65 ter 4130, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a meeting held by President Tudjman on the 23rd of August, 1995, with, among others, the minister of defence and the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 9 of the English, please, and this is page 17 of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at the top, it is Minister Jarnjak talking, at the top in the Croatian version. It is the upper middle part of the page in English. He says: "We have a significant drop in crime rights in Osijek and in that area; however, there's a huge problem that now after Storm and after Flash, there are now again so many weapons in private hands, explosives, uncontrolled, that simply, I don't know, we will now pass this law and we will have to launch a massive campaign for return of these weapons. Look, I know of rifle, automatic ones, anything you want." Then Mr. Susak says: "Mr. President, here, in a house, a private house, to get in there and find 100 kilograms of explosives, that's nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn the page in English, please, and in Croatian to turn the page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian, Ms. Botteri, it is Mr. Susak second from the bottom, that entry before the Ivan Jarnjak passage; and in English, it's at the top. It says: "Minister Susak, we are doing this without a law what we are doing with the mobilisation, because we're simply taking away by force. There is no law saying what you're allowed to do and what you're not. Then Jarnjak says: "There was a law passed stating what is allowed and what is not, but the problem is that nobody will report. Nobody will report anybody. You have plenty of grenades." Then General Cervenko says: "In the process of, Mr. President, in the process of demobilization, we had 15 people who were killed, up until now, 15 people." Then Cervenko continues on: "They throw grenades at each other and so forth. Fifteen people were killed until yesterday in the process of demobilization." Susak says: "Okay. These also include suicides, but, Mr. President, the outcome at the end of demobilization will more dead than in the operation. That has always been so in every operation we have." The president says: "Wait a moment. Are you demobilizing with weapons?" Cervenko says: "They hand in the weapons." Susak says: "But they hand in the weapons they were issued officially, Mr. President, what we had now in operation, especially the Home Guard and the reserves. They wouldn't report anything they took. We give him a rifle and he will return the rifle to us. But the fact that he took two more on top of that, that is something we have no record of." Ivan Jarnjak: "Then the right to these trophies and everything, the war booty and all that." Susak says: "That's no problem; it's logged."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you went a bit too quick for the transcriber --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was just listening to the French channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That doesn't help because the transcribe is the one who doesn't speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One the next page, Mr. Jarnjak says: "No, they don't log, that's the point." Susak says: "Yes, they don't log." Now, Ms. Botteri, are you able to help us with explaining what we just read about what the problems with demobilizing the Home Guard elements and the reservists -- do you know how they were able and where they were coming up with the weapons that the Croatian army itself could not keep track of, where they were getting weapons from?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me not repeat myself. I agree with the text that has just been read out; in other words, I believe that this could have involved war trophies, war booty; that's to say, weapons that were not registered or reported anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've heard testimony from a Prosecution witness named Ive Kardum, who talked about the fact that tons of explosives were found in the former so-called Krajina when the Croatian authorities took over. Are you familiar with the fact that -- these reservists when they entered the zone were able to discover weapons that were left behind by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. Although that was not an area I was concerned with, I had heard of a store house somewhere where such weapons were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm putting these questions to you because of the relationship to discipline that this issue would have. Was it, in fact, the case with reservists who were leaving or entering the zone, that the soldiers were acquiring weapons, unbeknownst to their commanders and the Croatian institutions? Are you familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And when Mr. Susak on this transcript talks about "the process of demobilization will result in more deaths than in the operation itself," are you able to help us with what he -- exactly he is referring to there in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see the text. What I can only conclude or assume is that Minister Susak has expressed his concern, anticipating exactly one such situation where soldiers who got hold of weapons that had not been officially registered anywhere could be responsible for precisely such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D890.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D890 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to follow up on that point, Your Honour. If I could have Exhibit D586, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the problems about the weapons and the problems, and that is in your last answer: "Soldiers who got hold of weapons that had not been officially registered anywhere could be responsible for precisely such incidents." Now, this is a letter from Josko Moric from the Ministry of Interior to Mr. Lausic, talking precisely about this issue. As you can see, he says: "We have received information that demobilization of a certain number of conscripts has begun and that soon a more extensive" mobilization "can be expected."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we will need to correct the translation there. It should say -- in the original Croatian, it says: "That soon a more extensive demobilization can be expected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "With the return of the HV units and the demobilization of conscripts, a certain quantity of weapons, ammunition, mines, explosives, and other deadly materiel has been brought to the previously liberated parts of our country. We estimate that the quantity of this materiel will increase once the planned number of conscripts has been fully demobilized."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The consequences of the arrival of new quantities of the materiel have already been demonstrated in the cases when it was used to violate public law and order, cause public danger, and attack authorised officials or prevent them from carrying out their duty." He then proposes a series of actions to be done between the MUP and military police concerning this process of demobilization. Now, disciplinary infractions that were issued concerning the misuse of weapons or disciplinary sanctions that were issued because of the misuse of weapons or taking weapons out of storage areas, which is another case that was shown to you on direct examination, was that also, those disciplinary measures, part of the effort? In other words, disciplinary measures to ensure that weapons were being properly stored and taken away from conscripts, was that your understanding at that time that that was part of the process of ensuring the return of law and order to the area?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 646, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now what appears to be an inspection of the Split Military District that had been conducted by Colonel General Zivko Budimir and his report of the inspection sent to the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, on the 18th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, please, and page two in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Budimir's inspection, under problems, he writes: "Lack of good and compatible means of communication, which significantly impedes the commanding of units, particularly during offensive operations." Then it continues on: "The problem ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The problem with regard to the means of communication is more apparent in reserve units that were mobilized shortly before the start of Operation Storm." Part b says: "Changes of command personnel in reserve units that were demobilized for a long period of time and commands and command personnel only recognise the real state within the units when in combat." Now, can you explain a little bit for us that -- those two paragraphs concerning reserve units? The reserve units themselves had been demobilized for a long period of time prior to Operation Storm, is that correct, many of the units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was true for a large number of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then there was a mass mobilization on the eve of Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Budimir notes that the commanders of these units who had been mobilized on the eve of Operation Storm only recognised the real state of the unit when the unit is in combat. Is that -- from your perspective or from your knowledge in the Split Military District, is that something that is consistent with your view about what commanders of reserve units really knew about what was going on in their units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D891, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D891 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Botteri, could I ask you one follow-up question. You were asked about whether what you saw in this document, that is, what the real state of these reserve units were, whether your view was consistent with what you find in these documents. What did you know about commanders of reserve units and their knowledge of the state of their units? What's the basis of your view on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my communication with them and from documentation that I received from various units, which I was then able to review and assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a rather vague answer. Could you be more concise, more concrete. You said your communication with them. What kind of communication you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean direct communication; that's to say, oral communication. I meant correspondence, written communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of correspondence would you receive in which these reserve units commanders would express their views on the difference between the state within the units, in combat and not in combat? What was it that caused them to communicate with you on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In more cases than one, this would not involve direct communication with individuals. Let me give you an example. A moment ago, I said that I was duty-bound to send reports on military discipline measures to my competent superior body. I had a deadline which, in turn, forced me to obtain timely reports from units, and I had difficulties in that. This was the sort of communication that I had with them. I had to make sure that I -- that they observed their deadlines in order for me to carry out my duties toward my superiors in a timely fashion. I had difficulties in carrying out my duties. That depended on their reports, and this was something that entailed my communication with commanders of reserve units, of reserve brigades. I don't know if I was clear enough this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you were very clear but not on the subject matter I asked you about. Could you give us an example of a communication from which you learned what you say was consistent with what you find in this document, an example of it. Not only that it was difficult to get everything there in time and to report in time and that you have problems with that, but just an example of a communication in which you were informed about how they viewed in combat times the real state within these units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer the specific question about what certain commanders thought of the status or situation in their respective units. I did not have direct knowledge of that; however, in my line of duty, I was able to arrive at a conclusion to the effect that this was, indeed, the situation that prevailed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, let's follow up on that -- on that issue. What do you know about -- let me ask the first question. Professional brigades were provided barracks, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about reserve brigades?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve brigades were, for the most part, relocated to various camps out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But reserve soldiers, when they were no longer on duty, did they go back to a barracks or did they go home?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These reserve brigades, they have fixed barracks facilities that were their permanent barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, at least, in part, you know that a commander of a reserve brigade would have a much harder time keeping track of his soldiers when they were' not in combat than, say, a commander of a professional brigade whose soldiers are being quartered in barracks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have -- and I have to use the ERN number. It is uploaded by the Prosecution into e-court, but there's no 65 ter number. It's 0354-2830.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report on disciplinary measures and sanctions you sent to the legal department on the 18th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please, and go to the third page in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the list of the table of disciplinary measures taken from the 1st of January, 1995, to the 30th of June, 1995. And if we scroll to the bottom of that page, we see that 1138 disciplinary measures were issued in that time-period. Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your statement, at your answer to question 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in the document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there are -- this report shows 261 proceedings conducted in one report, and in the attachment another 277 proceedings, and then attachment two shows 891 proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In total, when you add them all up, it appears that 1431 disciplinary proceedings were conducted in the third quarter, as opposed to 1138 disciplinary measures conducted in the first two quarters combined. My question is: Did you note the rise in the number of disciplinary measures in the third quarter back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since I was the one who sent these reports to the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding as to why more disciplinary measures were -- were being filed in the third quarter, as opposed to the first two quarters?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this was not something that one would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you have known why there was such a large number -- a large increase in the number of disciplinary measures in the third quarter?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the statistical data I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your statement refers to the fact that there were a greater number of mobilized members in the third quarter than there were in the first two.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was the increase in disciplinary measures in any way related to the increase in mobilized members in the third quarter?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was it about the reserve members that increased the number of disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reserve members were much less disciplined --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. My concentration seems to be on the decrease. Will we be having our break soon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could take a break. Perhaps that would be wise. Can you give us a further indication, then, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we resume at 25 minutes to 1.00, then what would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be done by about 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By about 1.00. Ms. Gustafson, would that cause you any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I expect I would need 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will are a break and resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there may have been good reasons why we are a bit late, I, nevertheless, apologise because it might influence the timing of the parties. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, the question I was posing to you at the end is that the reason that there were so many more disciplinary measures taken in the third quarter is because there were so many more mobilized soldiers in the third quarter. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were more mobilized soldiers and they were less disciplined. In my view, this resulted in a greater number of disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 1150, please. I'm sorry. I forgot to tender that into evidence. Your Honour, may I tender that document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D892.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's been pointed out to me, just for the record, that did have a 65 ter number, and it was 391. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then on the record as well. D892 is admitted into evidence. Could we ask one additional question. I noticed that in these statistics, we find two cases dealt with by the military disciplinary court in the third quarter. Could you explain why there were only two cases, which does not seems to be much, but perhaps you could explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's not on the screen. I think she's looking at the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not on the screen anymore. It was a similar statistic, and we find it on the ninth page, I think -- no. Let me just look at it. It's page 10 out of 12 of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must point out that, if accordance with the provisions of the Code of Military Discipline, a military procedure before a military disciplinary court could be instituted only for non-commissioned officers and officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm asking you because you say there's a limited number of people that were subject to this jurisdiction; nevertheless, the number of just two: One in category A, one in category C. It does not strike as a great productivity, but perhaps you could explain to us what explains this relatively low number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, there was a limited number of those against whom disciplinary proceedings could be substituted before a military disciplinary court, as I have just stated. Then the procedure itself was quite long and complex, and the cases depicted here are only those that have been finalised, which doesn't mean that there were not proceedings ongoing before the military disciplinary court at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does it mean that in the time that followed that number went up considerably, in accordance with the increased number of disciplinary measures being taken in the third quarter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that might have happened, and one could check that in the archives of the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, just as a clerical matter so that the record is clear, I think there is an issue as to whether the document I used and tendered is the same as 65 ter 391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I misspoke. It was 3391.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, again if I could have 65 ter 1150, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, this is a report issued by the legal affairs administration in Zagreb on the 15th of April, 1996. The subject is "Report on disciplinary measures and sentences imposed in the HV and criminal proceedings completed before military courts in the period from October to December 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of this report in the English. I'm not sure we have the right page. It should be -- in the Croatian, it should go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, reading page -- or the paragraph in the Croatian, paragraph 3, misnumbered in the English translation as a second paragraph 2, it says: "As can be concluded from the previous item, a large number of disciplinary proceedings was conducted. Most of them were conducted in the Split Military District, as many as 1257; while 1048 disciplinary measures were imposed in the Osijek Military District."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 8 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The conclusion in paragraph 1 says: "A large number of disciplinary proceedings were carried out in the period between October and December 1995. Large discrepancies, however, were observed in the number of disciplinary proceedings carried out and disciplinary measures pronounced in different military districts. These discrepancies should reflect the real state of affairs. "But if we take into consideration the fact that 1257 disciplinary measures were imposed in the Split Military District and none in the Gospic Military District, it is obvious that we are dealing here with different sentencing criteria, i.e., with different disciplinary policies in different military districts. Such a situation must be dealt with." Now, from this passage, Ms. Botteri, is it your reading of this document that the author of the document is using this -- is using the Split Military District as an example of a military district that is, in fact, processing a large number of disciplinary measures, in comparison with, for example, the Gospic Military District?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, not only compared to the Gospic Military District but with every other military district as well. My comment on this is that this reflects what I have been trying to depict in my statements here, and it reflects the situation and the extent to which there was insistence in the Split Military District on establishing military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Botteri, we've seen the statistics, we've seen that, in comparison with other Military Districts the Split Military District, at least in the fourth quarter, led in terms of the number of disciplinary measures taken. You were the person in charge in the command for legal affairs and keeping track of what was happening concerning the implementation of military discipline in the military district. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did there ever come a point in time where you, in reviewing the information that was coming into you, suspected that the system of military discipline was not functioning, that there was a problem in the system -- putting aside the recommendations you made in the letter on the 14th of August, in addition to those, was there any point in time where you said, "The system is broken or the system is not functioning"?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If something was not functioning in terms of the military disciplinary system, is it fair to say that it would have been your responsibility to alert General Gotovina and the members of the -- or your superiors in the legal affairs department in Zagreb, that something was not right, in terms of the functioning of the military disciplinary system?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever tell General Gotovina that there was any problem in the functioning of the military disciplinary system at any time between the 4th of August, 1995, and the end of December 1995, excluding, of course, the suggestions you made in the 14 August letter?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm instructed to read into the record that we're taking -- or to seek permission, I should say, to make a correction to a translation to an exhibit that we used yesterday. It is D879. We have collected the translation error and wish to put on the record that we will replace page 1D58-0039 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, did you have an opportunity to verify the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, not yet, Your Honour. This is the first I have heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the record and then the new copy will be the valid one, unless Ms. Gustafson reports to us before next Tuesday that there's any objection against the new translation. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was just wondering if Mr. Misetic wanted to tender that last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise and appreciate it. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's no objection. But because it relates to specifically to a question that Your Honour raised that the witness wasn't able to answer, the document indicates that there were four military disciplinary proceedings in the Split Military District disciplinary court for the fourth quarter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although this is argumentative rather than anything else, you explained to us the content which might not be appropriate. But if it is correct what Ms. Gustafson says, then I take it that you would agree that the mere mentioning that this not the way to proceed would suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P1007 on the screen, please, then if we could go to page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S, and if Article 9 could be expanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Botteri, I'd just like to you read to yourself Article 9 of the military disciplinary code.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It must be on the previous page in the B/C/S. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that this is a provision that deals with how disciplinary measures should be taken against officers and NCOs in state administrative bodies, businesses, and other legal entities, and that disciplinary measures should be imposed in accordance with the regulations in such bodies and disciplinary violations dealt with military disciplinary courts? Is that a fair reading?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could now go to D881.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, this document you're about to see, this is the set of proposals that was referred to earlier, proposals to the -- to amend the Code of Military Discipline. And as you go through this document, do you see that your proposals deal with the Code and it goes Article by Article, chronologically? So first a proposal to Article 3, then Article 4, then Article of, then Article 9, and so on. Is that how it's set out?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go, then, to the last paragraph in the B/C/S; and in the English, it's the first paragraph on page 2. Then if we could -- it should be the first page in B/C/S and the last paragraph. Sorry. And if we could expand the last paragraph so that the witness could read it more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is your proposal dealing with Article 9, paragraph 2, and the proposal is set out disciplinary responsibility proceedings and the powers of persons serving in the armed forces of the RH at headquarters, administrations regional departments, et cetera, that are not included in the present provisions of the Code. You note: "Since in our work to date we have had such cases, for example, violation of military discipline at the defence office, the headquarters, administration, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the top of the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Then this is a paragraph that you were referred to in cross-examination, where it says: "We think the simplest way to deal with disciplinary violations is to implement the principle of territoriality." Then you were asked about that. Then the next paragraph talks about changes to Article 9, paragraph 3 of the Code. Then further down the page, you can see there are proposals to Article 10, Article 11, Article 14, 15, 33, 34, and so on. Ms. Botteri, this paragraph at the top off page 2 here, is that a paragraph that's dealing with proposals to amend Article 9 of the Code?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you were asked about there in cross-examination, you said: "What we want to the achieve was the following: The added tasks that were not in the organic composition, and we've often discussed this in the course of my testimony, should also be been the competence of the commander of the Split Military District as regards military discipline. So all the attached units would be under his command as regards military discipline. That was our proposal." Ms. Botteri, it's correct from our reading of Article 9 that had has nothing to do with attached subordinate the units. Article 9 deals with officers and NCOs working in certain administrative bodies, businesses, and legal entities. So my question is: If this was your intention to ensure that attached units would be under the disciplinary authority of the military district commander, why did you make that proposal here in the context of an amendment to Article 9?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you to put the text of the Article back on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was P1007. I believe it was on page 3 in B/C/S, or possibly page 2, and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can go back now to the text of my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. Could we go back to D881.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, you will recall that it was the last paragraph on page 1, the paragraph at the bottom of your screen.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal, as regards Article 9, was -- it referred to a different category of persons than the one I was referring to in the passage on territorial responsibility. Article 9, that is, of the Code of Military Discipline, in the first two items, speaks of the imposition of disciplinary measures; and in item 2 of the same Article, an exception is made, and it is stated that disciplinary proceedings can be instituted against such persons according to the rules of the institutions these persons are working in. In item 3 of Article 9, there is reference to the breaches of discipline that those persons have committed, the major breaches. In practice, the implementation of the Article defined in this way was unclear, which is why I asked for that Article to be amended and to be defined with greater precision. In relation to the jurisdiction of the military disciplinary court for the major breaches of discipline of those persons, I even proposed that those persons be enumerated, listed. In contrast to the proposals for amendments to Article 9, the proposed amendments, as regards the application of the territorial principle, referred to a proposal that this principle be applied for both major and minor breaches of discipline; and in my interpretation, these are two different proposals, two different situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you maintain that this paragraph deals with the territorial principle being applied to attached subordinated units, even though Article 9 doesn't deal with attached subordinated units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the claim that it doesn't deal with attached subordinated units. Paragraph 1 is a very broad --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking that exact question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- well, let me just read it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the objection. The witness agreed with me earlier on that paragraph 9 did deal with the particular people mentioned in that Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree that it deals with that in section 2, but it doesn't mean that deals with other things in section 1 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you rephrase the question such that Mr. Misetic's objection does not apply anymore and you get the answer that you're seeking.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, the first paragraph on page 2, does that address the problem that you claim existed with attached subordinated units? Is that paragraph proposing an amendment so that attached subordinated units are under the disciplinary authority of the district that they're attached to?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The first paragraph on page 2, at the top of the page in front of you.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your specific question in relation to -- or, rather, your specific question is related to that first paragraph on page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The first paragraph on page 2, does that address the problem that you said existed with attached subordinated units? Is that paragraph proposing an amendment so that attached subordinated units are under the disciplinary authority of the district that they're attached to?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you explain why that paragraph is in between a proposed amendment to Article 9, paragraph 2, and Article 9, paragraph 3, when Article 9, paragraph 2, deals with the disciplinary responsibility of certain individuals working for certain entities and doesn't deal with attached subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you clarify it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- in light of the limit the time I have, I'd just like to move on at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, you were asked about parallel disciplinary and criminal investigations, and you were asked to interpret Article 31 of the Code. You gave certain answers, and I'd just like to clarify those answers with a concrete answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 5990.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, can you see that this is it a special report of the military police relating to an event, an incident that occurred on the 21st of May in front of the Trogir police station. It describes what took place at approximately 2005 hours. It was reported that a hand-grenade was thrown in front of the Trogir police station by some 100 members of the 114th Brigade. One person was seriously injured and a vehicle was damaged. Now, Trogir, that's on the coast near Split. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just scroll through the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We can see there is a chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, and if we go then to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The last paragraph indicates that the identify of the perpetrator was revealed, and it's reported that a forensic investigation is under way with the aim of apprehending the above-mentioned. You can see it is signed by Major Budimir. Does it appear to you that in relation to this incident a criminal proceeding is under way?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to 65 ter number 2110.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a document also from the 22nd of May, the same date. It says that on the basis of a specific incident which took place on in Trogir on the 21st of May, members of the Croatian army committed several unmilitary and legally punishable crimes, which resulted with severe consequences of life and health of a civilian and with big damage. Then there's an order, and it's an order to the commander of VP 2136, which is the 114th Brigade, to immediately constitute a commission, to investigate the causes and consequences of the incident, and under point 3, to take the strictest measures against the perpetrators of the incident. If you go to the next page, you can see it's an order from General Gotovina to the commander of the 114th Brigade. Now, in your cross-examination, you were asked: "Was there a potential that by launching a parallel investigation," it was in reference to a parallel disciplinary investigation, "you could disrupt evidence in the criminal investigation?" You said: "Of course." My question to you is: Can you explain in relation to this example how a parallel disciplinary investigation could disrupt the evidence in a parallel criminal investigation? What was the concern?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigations conducted for the purposes of military disciplinary procedures were led by either individuals or commissions consisting of members who were not specially trained for that job. The military police had a specialist department and staff who were especially trained for that job. Therefore, the conduct of parallel investigations could cause such problems, and frequently so. In some cases, this ultimately proved to be a fruitless exercise if, within the military police force, there were -- there was personnel who dealt particularly with that sort of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you give me one concrete example of how a disciplinary investigation could disrupt a parallel criminal proceedings? I'm talking in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me too much. So much time has elapsed that I don't remember any specific examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked some questions about statistics and the provision and availability of statistical information on disciplinary measures at the Split Military District. In one of those, you confirmed that you had no statistical information whatsoever for units that were temporarily operationally subordinated to the Split Military District. Then you were asked: "Now, when we talk about what types of problems did the non-territoriality create, would one of the problems be that the Split Military District commander -- command," sorry, "was not entitled to receive information about disciplinary measures being undertaken by units that are operating on its territory?" Then you said: "Correct. That's what I said. We were unable to control, supervise, or evaluate the situation." Now, in terms of the Split Military District being entitled to receive information, my question is: In relation to, for example, the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade, which was operationally subordinated to the Split Military District but organically a part of the Gospic Military District, if General Gotovina had requested information from General Norac in the Gospic Military District and requested General Norac to provide him with statistics or other information on disciplinary measures being imposed on members of the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade, do you think that that is a request that General Norac would have complied with?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "would have complied with"? He would probably react by saying that that was not standard procedure. What are you exactly referring to? Reports on disciplinary measures imposed or some sort of information or brief? I don't quite understand what you have in mind there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: For example, the statistical information that you received, statistical information on a quarterly basis, if General Gotovina had requested that information for the units of the 2nd Battalion of the 9th Guards Brigade from the Gospic Military District, do you think he would have been able to receive that information?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that there would arise such a situation for that sort of information to be sought in this particular manner, if we know what sort of system was in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, could I ask you one question. You explained to us that it was problematic that you could not keep matters under control because there was no information about disciplinary matters taken against members of temporarily subordinated units belonging to another military district. Ms. Gustafson would like to know whether that information could have been obtained from, for example, the Gospic Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In practice, a situation where we would be seeking that information would not arise, if a system was in place where the Gospic Military District reported to the competent administration for legal matters of the ministry on issues concerning its personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was ever an effort made to obtain that information? You've got a lot of units under your temporary command or temporarily under your command. Now, you know that you've got no knowledge whatsoever about any disciplinary measures taken about members of those units. Was ever an effort made to obtain that information, because I do understand that the lack of information bothered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have reason to doubt that the system functioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but we sought that information from the competent administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you make an effort to get that about disciplinary measures, for example, the units you mentioned before, to obtain that information from the Gospic Military District, through whatever way? Did you seek that information, did you make an effort to obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just finally, Ms. Botteri, I have a similar question in relation to the questions were asked about the practice of imposing in informal disciplinary measures by simply demobilizing soldiers who were problematic. Yo. You were asked whether you had any -- whether these individual demobilizations would be reflected in any of the statistics, and you said no. Then you were asked where they wouldn't be in your statistics, and you said that that wasn't part of the -- that wasn't provided for in the Code of Military Discipline. My question is a similar to the one His Honour just posed: Was a request ever made, to your knowledge, to obtain information on how many soldiers were being demobilized informally for reasons of misconduct or why soldiers were being demobilized, in terms of what the conduct was? Are you aware of any request like that, or order?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Let's start with some very practical matters. No number has yet been assigned to 65 ter 01150. I think you tendered it, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was no objection, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D893.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D893 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That reminds me, Your Honour, I neglected to get numbers for 65 ter 5990, which is also not on the 65 ter list, and 2110. Those were the two documents just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit number P1018, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit number P1019, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1018 and P1019 are admitted into evidence. I have a few questions for you, Ms. Botteri. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained, in the statement that you have given to the Defence, how the higher number of disciplinary measures could be explained in the third quarter of 1995. I will literally read what you said, where you explained that there were was a new system, you also explained that some units were missing in the reports, and you then said: "When you look at it this way, it turns out that the third quarter showed 25 percent more disciplinary proceedings than in the entire past six months. I remember the information is that we had 50 per cent more disciplinary proceedings per month in the third quarter of 1995 than in the past period." You said: "50 per cent more disciplinary proceedings per month." Is that, over the three months, 50 per cent more than over the three preceding months; or how should I understand the 50 per cent? I will read it again to you: "I remember the information is that we had 50 per cent more disciplinary proceedings per month in the third quarter of 1995 than in the past period." What do you mean exactly? Let's keep it very concrete. The third quarter is July, August, September. Now tell us what was 50 percent more in July, August, September; whether July or August or September; or end August and September? Explain to me exactly what you mean there.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that what I meant was that there were 50 per cent more in that particular quarter, the third quarter, as compared to the previous three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you state that it turned out that the third quarter showed 25 percent more disciplinary proceedings than in the entire past six months, can you --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember the figure of 25 percent. In which of the statements did I say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the last statement. It's one line before the 50 percent.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer concerning the 25 percent at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question. You emphasised, as you said in your statement given to the Defence, that even if people were demobilized as a kind of a sanction for inappropriate disorderly behaviour, that, of course, there was still criminal liability. Could you give us any example of someone who was, for the reason of disorderly behaviour or inappropriate behaviour, demobilized? Do you have remember any such case, specific case?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such cases. I wasn't in charge of demobilization, nor did I receive reports on demobilization. As far as I remember, some of the documents were shown to us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you have any knowledge whether before someone was demobilized for such inappropriate behaviour, whether that behaviour was investigated and whether there were any reports made in that respect?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell me which report you're referring to, the one in the military disciplinary procedure or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that demobilization was encouraged and was a quasi-sanction. Now, was this usually, as far as you know, investigated and were the results of such an investigation, in whatever context, put on paper when such a person was demobilized.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific one, even if not by name, an event you may remember?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a specific one, no; but there were such case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that even if someone was demobilized, that, of course, you would like to emphasise that all soldiers were always as criminally liable as any other citizen of the Republic of Croatia. Do you know of any concrete case where someone, because of bad behaviour, was demobilized but then brought before a court, in order to establish whether there was any criminal liability for misconduct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is beyond dispute that every such demobilized soldier incurred criminal liability, but I do not recall specific cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not challenge your statement about criminal liability; I was asking about a concrete example. I have no further questions for you. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Misetic, a brief question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes, and with the indulgence of the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I think the interpreters as well. First, Mr. President, I will deal with your question later. I believe there's cases in evidence already about soldiers who were demobilized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I just wanted to look at the knowledge of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in relation to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Further cross-examination by Mr. Misetic:

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, quickly, the issue of you not asking for reports of reports of people who were demobilized, you didn't ask for them because you did not have a legal objection --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was not a question, Your Honour; it was whether any request was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not the sure what --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked about whether reports were made about the behaviour which caused --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was asking something about Ms. Gustafson's question earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The question was: Was there a request ever made to your knowledge; it wasn't whether the witness made such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, a request by the Split Military District for that information would haven't about necessary for the purposes of the statistics because you weren't under a legal obligation to provide the statistics of demobilized soldiers to Zagreb, were you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have repeatedly emphasised that this was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So, now to my next point, which is this issue about territoriality the principle of territoriality, did anyone from Zagreb in the legal affairs department ever come and contact you and say, "Ms. Botteri, we're not getting any statistics from you about disciplinary measures being taken by attached units. You're required to give us those statistics when they're attached to your military district"? Did anybody ever -- in the years you worked in the district, did anyone ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. May I take it that other Defence counsel that the questions by the Bench have not triggered the need to put any further questions to the witness. Then I have to deal with another rather practical matter, which is that we were informed that neither the Markac or the Cermak Defence object against the Prosecution's proposed bar table submissions. What is the position of the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. This leads me to the following: Ms. Gustafson, I think there was some guidance of the Chamber about how to present bar table submissions about what we had to look at specifically, because we - I'll just give an example - we have heard questions put to this witness in relation to all these statistics, first six months, last quarter, 18th of October, then a new report, 25th of October, and then another report on 10th of November, all about the same substance. These documents, the 18th of October we have had extensively on our screens, I don't know whether -- I don't think that the others were tendered into evidence. Now I see on your list the 18th of October, 1995; that is, 3391. We also see the supplementary report on disciplinary matters and sanctions of 25th of October. The 10th of November report, is that also somewhere? Can we find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was admitted, Your Honour, and the 18th of October was admitted in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, it's finally only the 25th of October which gives the additional numbers. The Chamber has never seen that document. The Chamber, therefore, is also not in the position to see whether all the calculations made, I would say, in the Defence statement, reference is made there under ERN numbers to numbers of disciplinary measures. The Chamber is not in a position to verify, until after this witness leaves this courtroom, which is not only because I'm often focussing on concrete information, but we are not in a position to that, if we proceed this way, because it's introduced in the OTP statements. It's then further dealt with in paragraphs 28, 29, 30, where reference is made to it in question, I think, 19 in the Defence statement. We are there, and we read about ERN numbers and we have no possibility even in preparing for the testimony of this witness to verify, for example, the numbers 25 percent, 50 per cent, what periods of time. We just don't know. So, therefore, we should find one way or another a solution so that, apart from the parties understanding the evidence for the full 100 percent, that the Chamber who will finally have to make determinations is also in a position to fully and in every detail verify the evidence. That being said, the Registrar is invited to assign numbers, after having consulted with Ms. Gustafson, to the documents appearing on the Botteri bar table exhibit lists; and once this has been done and once those that are not needed to be admitted into evidence anymore are stricken from the list, the Chamber will beside on the matter. I am aware that there are a few other procedural issues pending, urgent issues pending. Unfortunately, we can't spend any time on it today anymore, so we'll leave that for next Monday. Meanwhile, Ms. Botteri, knowing that you're a lawyer, otherwise I would have asked Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom, but to give you some additional insight in proceedings before this Chamber, I'd like to thank you very much for having answered the questions put to you by the parties and put to you by this Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until Monday, the 3rd of November, 9.00, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
